items.title: This Is What Women’s Self-Defense Looks Like
items.description: This article was featured in the One Story to Read Today newsletter. Sign up for it here. O n the first day of self-defense class, I learn to say “no.” We’re in a Southern California martial-arts studio not far from an In-N-Out Burger. The space smells faintly of cooked meat. I’m one of six students, all women: four nurses, one flight attendant, and me. In this introductory session, we’re supposed to get a taste of what it means to protect ourselves—and, if necessary, to fight back. For the longest time, I had wondered what it would be like to hit someone. Like, really hit them. I had grown up understanding that women aren’t supposed to engage in fantasies about violence, which is to say that we aren’t really supposed to think about it. But many of us do. All the time. Violence can, of course, affect anyone. It is in our homes and neighborhoods and in the news; it is experienced person to person, nation to nation, directly and indirectly. But for women especially, even when violence is not an immediate physical reality, what is real is the constant threat of it . In my experience, this sense of threat doesn’t change as time goes on. So in late 2023, I signed up for self-defense classes with a training program called Impact Personal Safety. I was working on a book exploring the ways in which women and girls are socialized not to say “no,” even to people who threaten them. But I also just wanted to understand what it is for “no” to be expressed in the body—what it means to feel the “no.” Our lead instructor, Dawn Hofmeister, is in her 50s and petite. She stands straight and appears to glide through the air, and although I’m much larger than she is, I feel submissive in her presence. She teaches alongside a couple of female assistants and a male sparring partner, Matt Harris. A middle-aged man with doe-like eyes, Harris tells the assembled group that he will be playing the role of our assailant that day, a character named Billy. Everyone likes Harris. Nobody likes Billy. Billy emerges after Harris slips on a padded suit and helmet. In the scenarios we’re thrown into, Billy is aggressive. He walks right at us, his voice raised. He can also be sneaky: Sometimes, he’ll sidle up in a bumbling, faux-friendly way before lunging. Other times, he appears to be severely mentally ill, or under the influence of drugs, or perfectly sober but intensely pushy. He asks for things (the time, a cellphone) or whether we need something—help with our groceries? A ride? When we rebuff him, he starts toward us with purpose. “No!” we yell. This is supposed to come after some effort at placating him— I don’t need a ride, thank you ; I think the person you’re looking for went the other way —a tactic that, in these scenarios, does not work, in that it does not thwart Billy from approaching, bull-like, with apparent malicious intent. Hofmeister explains that she teaches students to say “no” repeatedly and often because it helps strengthen a woman’s resolve to assert her boundaries and puts a potential assailant on notice that what he’s about to do is undesired. She adds that the word can increase the power of a physical blow and disrupt a freeze response, keeping the woman breathing through her counterattack. Along with saying “no,” we’re taught the palm-heel strike—heels of the hands up and together, palms facing outward, ready to hit—the first line of physical defense in a sequence of moves and postures meant to end with Billy on his back or side, writhing. The second move is a strong knee to the groin. The third, once he’s down, is a knee or stomp to the head. Billy takes a fair amount of abuse. Sometimes I worry about Harris, the human being inside the padded suit, especially when he is slow to get back on his feet. But feeling bad for Billy, I realize, is part of what I’m trying to undo: the internalized empathy response that can make people, especially women, afraid to hit another person, or lead them to give bad actors the benefit of the doubt even while the voice in their own head is saying danger . When Billy advances toward us, my first “no” is the weakest. But then my hands go up and I yell “No!” with more force. Billy falls, and I jab my heel into his chin. My knee goes to his groin—another “No!” Soon the no ’s are coming quickly and easily, and by the time Billy is splayed on the ground, I’m hovering over him—like Muhammad Ali standing over Sonny Liston in that famous 1965 photo—and practically screaming. C ontemporary self-defense courses recognize that protecting oneself involves a lot more than elbowing an assailant in the neck. As Susan Brownmiller put it in her 1975 book, Against Our Will: Men, Women and Rape , telling women to kick a man in the groin or stick a thumb in his eye is not enough—because first, women must overcome an aversion to hitting. Describing her time learning self-defense, she wrote that this inhibition “was so strong in each of us that on the first try none of us could make physical contact.” What women need, she argued, “is systemic training in self-defense that begins in childhood, so that the inhibition resulting from the prohibition may be overcome.” What many people think of as women’s self-defense tends to go by the designation Empowerment Self-Defense, or ESD. Also known as “feminist self-defense” and “holistic self-defense,” ESD posits that teaching nonphysical strategies is as important as teaching physical ones—because if a woman can recognize and thwart an attacker’s verbal intrusions early in an encounter, she is less likely to need to get physical. Impact Personal Safety, Southern California, the program I trained under, says that it has taught assertiveness, boundary-setting, deflection, and de-escalation to tens of thousands of students—plus the skills necessary for what the organization’s late founder, Lisa Gaeta, described as “causing a scene.” (Essentially: raising your voice and shouting things such as “Get away from me” and “I don’t want this,” which is harder to do than you might think.) That makes ESD different from mainstream self-defense, which “tends to be stranger-focused, sometimes fear-based, rather than empowerment-based,” Jocelyn Hollander, a University of Oregon sociology professor and self-defense instructor, told me. ESD’s emphasis on “internal” skills—emotional, psychological—is aimed at subverting behaviors that students might have adopted based on their gender or personal history, or in response to political and cultural messaging. Basically, Hollander said, the method gives women the tools they need to say no “to whatever someone wants to do to or with you.” ESD is applicable not only in extreme interactions but also in what some might call the more routine situations that many women experience, such as being coerced into sex. In Hollander’s classes, she has students turn to each other with a simple question—“Can I borrow your pencil?” or “Do you want to go have coffee?”—to which the other person then has to respond “No.” Usually, there’s a lot of nervous laughter, Hollander told me. Many students realize that they never say “no” to anybody. Or, when they do, they qualify it, soften it, make excuses. But once they discover that the world won’t end when they say “no,” Hollander observed, it can be a “huge epiphany.” Such training, Hollander’s research suggests, pays tangible dividends. Women who take ESD classes are less likely to be the victim of rape or sexual assault than women who do not. In a 2020 study of female college students involving nearly 300 women, Hollander found that those who had taken an ESD class had about 50 percent lower odds, on average, of experiencing any sort of assault over the one-year period following the course than those who had not taken a class. “I just have to point out that 50 percent is a huge decrease for an intervention,” she said. “Psychologists are usually happy if they get a few percentage points’ difference. Fifty percent is immense.” Her research has also found that many students experience increased “self-efficacy”—a sense that they can be effective in the world. And other research has found that this sort of self-defense training can reduce feelings of anxiety, depression, fear, and self-blame. Hollander’s results have been echoed in the work of other academics, including Charlene Senn, a University of Windsor psychology professor whose research focuses on male violence against women. Senn was inspired by the academics Patricia Rozee and Mary Koss, who in 2001 published a paper titled “ Rape: A Century of Resistance ,” which synthesized decades of research on sexual violence. They translated their analysis into a series of recommendations, such as giving women cognitive and emotional education to defend themselves against assault. Senn took those recommendations and set out to make them come alive. First, she created a program for university women called Enhanced Assess, Acknowledge, Act—a 12-hour, evidence-based training that, among other things, teaches women how to recognize a risk of sexual assault and then resist it. Then, from 2011 to 2013, she and a group of academics conducted a study of 893 female college freshmen in Canada, to test the program’s efficacy. Of the students, 451 were assigned to a “resistance group” and took EAAA classes, and 442 were put in a control group, which meant that they basically “went to a room,” Senn said, and read sexual-assault-prevention pamphlets distributed by their schools. [ Read: A recipe for sexual assault ] After the EAAA courses, Senn said, the resistance and control groups were given follow-up surveys at intervals of one week, six months, 12 months, and 18 months. The researchers found that one year after the EAAA training, the women in the resistance group were 46.3 percent less likely to have been raped and 63.2 percent less likely to have experienced attempted rape than the women in the control group. A later study by Senn and her colleagues, which looked at a broader, more diverse cohort of university women who took EAAA classes from 2017 to 2021, had similar findings: a 57.3 percent reduction in reports of rape and a 32.9 percent reduction in attempted rape six months after the training. To me, these results were nothing short of stunning. I wondered why data like these hadn’t been publicized more widely. Jill Cermele, a psychology professor at Drew University, told me that this was partly because of ideology. Cermele co-authored a 2022 paper with Martha McCaughey, an academic specializing in women’s studies and the author of Real Knockouts: The Physical Feminism of Women’s Self-Defense , about the ways in which the efficacy of self-defense has been neglected or ignored by both public-health officials and anti-rape activists—some of whom contend that emphasizing the need for women to learn self-defense serves only to put the onus on them, rather than on men. Cermele said she believes that this logic is misguided—that no matter people’s views on blame, anyone who cares about women’s safety has “a professional and a moral obligation to pay attention to the data.” That said, “one of the things that psychology tells us is that people are not convinced by data—they’re convinced by stories.” D uring my next set of self-defense classes, things take a darker turn. The 16-hour “basics” training unfolds over the course of two weekends, with a new cohort of students. Our lead instructor is Dani, a young woman who took her first Impact class when she was only 6. Our padded assailant is Michael Peñafiel, a middle-aged father of a young son. Like Harris, our attacker from the intro class, Peñafiel has an alter ego: Kane. On Day 1, we hit, we kick, we send knees into Kane’s groin. Yet the stakes feel somehow lower. Partly, it’s the absurdity of Kane’s outfit—a suit of hard plastic, foam, and duct tape, with a harness-like thing slung between his legs and around his waist. His helmet makes him look like a bug. The padding forces hims to move around the studio with his hips thrust forward. But then comes Day 2: what we glibly call “sexual-assault day.” Our instructors teach us how to fend off an assailant who approaches while we’re lying on our side, and demands that we get into positions that could—quickly, disturbingly, unmistakably—leave us open to assault. We get down on hands and knees. We lie flat on our backs. Today, our attacker is closer, the interaction more intimate. This makes everything scarier and can provoke a freeze response that feels impossible to overcome. [ Read: Everything we know about rape is wrong ] Kane gets behind me, clutches my arms, and pins me to the floor. He crouches on his knees, breathing heavily over me. I think: Maybe if I just lie here, he will go away . I’m surprised at how heavy he is and how difficult it is to imagine freeing myself from his grasp. He hisses instructions. “What’s going on?” I ask him. We’re supposed to say this phrase out loud, not so much to prompt a reasonable answer but to remind ourselves that we are being attacked in the first place. He merely mumbles. Dani tells me to roll onto my back, which is the last thing I want to do. “Be patient,” she says. “He’s going to make a mistake.” And make a mistake he does. As Kane tries to position himself directly on top of me, he releases one of my arms and up it goes, my fingers in a beak-like shape, directed at his eyes. “Eyes! Eyes! Eyes!” everyone yells. I stab at the netting on his padded helmet, and Kane falls backward. Then I get into a kick position, leg in the air and ready to strike—his head, his torso, his groin, wherever I can find a target. After a few kicks, Kane finally goes down, at which point I pull myself up and run around to the top of his head to assess that he’s indeed knocked out. Finally, I run away, keeping in mind the final step: go get help. I should acknowledge that self-defense techniques may not help in situations when it is impossible or dangerous for a woman to fight back—such as when she is incapacitated, or when an assailant is armed and threatening deadly force. And it is fair to argue that the potential perpetrators of violence, not their victims, should be the ones subject to intervention and training. But Impact’s founder, Gaeta, who died last year, had no patience for the argument that to avoid victim blaming, women should not be taught to defend themselves. People say, “Well, we should make men be better,” she once told me. “How the fuck am I going to make men be better?” [ Read: Not all men, but any man ] The point about responsibility is not a new argument. In the ’80s and ’90s, for instance, some feminist activists began to express concern that teaching women self-defense was akin to engaging in victim blaming —so the practice became “unfashionable in a way,” Hollander told me. She added that yes, ideally, more men would move through life with the explicit understanding that they should not assault women, “but from a researcher’s perspective, we have no clue how to make that happen.” No intervention has been shown to meaningfully reduce perpetration. “And what are we supposed to do in the meantime?” Hollander said. “Just sit around and wait for the revolution?” Some researchers argue that when it comes to men, self-defense training for women can move the needle in an important way—by shifting men’s own understanding of their place in the world. “Changing men does not necessarily entail intervening directly with men,” Hollander wrote in a 2018 article. Quoting a paper by the masculinity researcher Michael Flood, she added, “Empowering women may transform gender relations by ‘shifting the wider conditions within which men make choices about violence and non-violence.’” T he third day of basics class is the day I start crying. We’re learning how to react defensively and offensively: Many of the techniques involve moving toward our assailant, not away from him. This is counterintuitive—instinctively, one wants to retreat from danger—but being able to inflict real damage and disable an attacker means having to get up close. The disabling doesn’t go well for me. About three hours into the class, I’m thrown to the mat and pinned. Kane is on top of me and feels stronger and heavier than usual, more hell-bent on restraining me. Just when I think I’ve started to get away, he grabs me again and pins me on my side, my back to him, my arms folded in front of me. I freeze. The instructors and other students yell words of encouragement—“He’s going to make a mistake!” someone calls—but I can’t move. The words are meaningless. Adrenalin is making me tremble. After what seems like an eternity, Kane seems to ease up a bit, and I’m able to turn toward him, hit him, and stumble away. I make my way to Gaeta—present that day, watching from a table at one end of the studio—who asks, “What happened?” The question is part of the drill. After the fight, we’re supposed to describe in as much detail as possible what occurred and what our attacker looked like, to practice how, in the real world, we might give specific information about an assault to a friend or law-enforcement officer. I’m not sure what to tell her, but I try: “He attacked me. He threw me to the ground. I tried to get up and almost succeeded, but he pinned me back down.” I feel shame and embarrassment rising, and I begin to cry. I run to the line of students assembled against a wall. One says, “Good job.” The others don’t know what to say. Neither do I. I just stand there with tears streaming, my heart thumping. Two weeks after my graduation from the class, I’m stuck on that memory, of an encounter that felt like failure. Peñafiel has since clarified that he did not, in fact, ease up on me. He also said that my reaction—freezing, crying—is not uncommon. Driving home from that class, shaken, I had called my friend Nancy, a documentary filmmaker whose work has focused largely on sexual assault. She tried to put what had happened to me into perspective: I got scared, she said, and felt shame and embarrassment, which came not only from being scared but also from my sense that I hadn’t fought back in the “right” way. About a week after the class, I also spoke with one of Impact’s assistant instructors, Amanda Hall, who is also a reality-TV producer. She told me that she has seen this sort of response many times. She herself cried during the opening drill in her first class. The adrenaline can be “really activating,” she said. “It’s scary no matter what.” I try to give myself a little grace. After all, I was able to finish the fight. This reminds me of something that Cermele, the psychology professor, told me: Many people mistakenly believe that once an assault happens or starts, you have to somehow wait until the assailant is finished. This is not always the case. “Unfortunately, assaults take time,” she said, which means “multiple opportunities for resistance. And if I couldn’t organize myself to resist in the beginning, if I was too drunk, if I was too afraid, if I was whatever, there might still be a moment where I can do something with that. And I think we miss that by not talking about resistance. It’s very all-or-nothing.” She told me about a student who, after learning self-defense techniques one semester, was assaulted by a male friend’s roommate at a college party. During the attack, the woman was able to summon her skills and fight him off. “We would call that a success story,” Cermele said. “The assault ended because of what she did, not because he decided it was over.” I now know what it feels like to hit someone. I also can’t stop thinking about how different the world might be if more girls and women were taught to defend themselves. We might see the number of assaults against women cut in half. We might see more teenagers like a self-defense student who told me that now she knows how to use her voice: “I feel like I’m a powerful person.” We would see more women learning to shout “No!” and enjoying, with much less fear, what one instructor called “a bigger life”—the kind of life every one of us deserves. ​​When you buy a book using a link on this page, we receive a commission. items.title: Mali : une première opération réussie pour séparer des bébés siamois
items.description: Une equipe medicale pluridisciplinaire malienne a realise avec succes une intervention chirurgicale visant a separer deux nourrissons siamois au Centre hospitalier universitaire (CHU) Gabriel-Toure de Bamako. L'operation, realisee 9 septembre, constitue une premiere dans le pays. Les deux fillettes sont nees le 29 août par cesarienne, au terme d'une grossesse au cours de laquelle des malformations congenitales avaient ete diagnostiquees. Elles etaient reliees par leurs systemes urinaire et digestif et partageaient notamment une meme vessie et un meme colon. Face a cette situation rare, le directeur general du CHU Gabriel-Toure, le professeur Thierno Madani Diop, a mobilise une equipe composee notamment de chirurgiens pediatriques, d'anesthesistes-reanimateurs, de cardiologues, de radiologues, de pharmaciens, de laborantins et de personnels paramedicaux du bloc operatoire. Apres plusieurs examens et diagnostics preoperatoires, les specialistes ont procede a l'intervention, dont le succes a ete salue par la ministre de la Sante et du Developpement social, Assa Badiallo Toure. Lors d'une visite au CHU, la ministre a qualifie l'intervention de « prouesse » et salue le travail des praticiens maliens. Selon les estimations citees par le ministere, les naissances de bebes siamois surviennent dans environ un cas sur 200 000 naissances. Cette reussite constitue une etape importante pour la medecine specialisee dans le pays et illustre les capacites des equipes medicales maliennes a prendre en charge des interventions chirurgicales complexes. Les jumeaux siamois apparaissent lorsqu'un embryon unique ne se separe pas completement au debut de la grossesse. La possibilite de les separer depend notamment des organes qu'ils partagent.

items.title: Boulkiemdé/Kindi : La mairie vole au secours des personnes vulnérables
items.description: BURKINA-BOULKIEMDE-KINDI-PERDONNES-VULNERABLES-SOUTIEN Boulkiemdé/Kindi : La mairie vole au secours des personnes vulnérables Kindi, 13 sept. 2026 (AIB) – La mairie de la commune rurale de Kindi a procédé le vendredi 11 septembre, à la remise de vivres au profit des personnes vulnérables de la localité, a constaté l'AIB. Composé de 44 sacs de maïs, de 21 sacs de riz de 25 kg et de 22 bidons d'huile de 5 litres, ce don est destiné aux veuves, aux personnes vivant avec un handicap ainsi qu'aux personnes déplacées internes (PDI). La cérémonie de remise a été présidée par le 2e vice-président, Bassolé, représentant le président de la délégation spéciale de Kindi, assisté du responsable du service social de la commune, Hamidou Kaboré. L’autorité communale a salué la résilience des bénéficiaires du jour tout en réitérant le soutien indéfectible de la municipalité à leur endroit. Elle a également salué le travail et le dévouement du service social aux côtés des couches vulnérables. Au nom des bénéficiaires, le responsable des personnes vivant avec un handicap, Barthélémy Zongo, a exprimé sa profonde gratitude à la mairie. Il a qualifié ce geste d'inestimable en cette période de soudure, tout en exhortant les autorités administratives à pérenniser et à multiplier de telles actions de solidarité à ces populations ne disposant pratiquement pas d'autres sources de soutien. Agence d'information du Burkina CS/PB/AS/ATA

items.title: Boulkiemdé/Thiou : les autorités administratives rendent hommage aux membres du district de la Police avant leur départ pour la réorganisation des forces de sécurité
items.description: BURKINA-BOULKIEMDE-THIOU-DEPART-POLICE-NATIONALE Boulkiemdé/Thiou : les autorités administratives rendent hommage aux membres du district de la Police avant leur départ pour la réorganisation des forces de sécurité Thiou, 13 Sept. 2026 (AIB) – Au cours d'une cérémonie solennelle de montée des couleurs nationales, les autorités administratives ont témoigné leur reconnaissance aux membres du district de la police de Thiou dans le cadre de leur départ. Cette cérémonie a commencé par la montée des couleurs accompagnée de l'exécution du Ditanyè. Le PDS, Rateba Dawega, a, après son mot de bienvenue, appelé à la citoyenneté, à l'amour de la patrie et au soutien des FDS et VDP. Pour lui, la police a toujours été un vent favorable pour le bon déroulement des activités de la mairie et dans la collaboration avec la population. D'où sa reconnaissance à ce corps paramilitaire qui n'a eu de cesse dans l'exercice salutaire, de la tâche à elle confiée. Pour le Commissaire, Hubert Koama, c'est vraiment un honneur de partager ces moments avec la population. Il a réaffirmé son engagement et sa disponibilité pour le bien de la Commune. Il a remercié les autorités pour cet honneur et félicité les appelés à l'immersion patriotique pour leur preuve de patriotisme dans les activités depuis leur Sortie. Les différents chefs de services (santé animale, environnement, inspection primaire, lycée départemental, CVD ) ont tour à tour, témoigné leur reconnaissance sur la bonne collaboration avec la police et souhaité une bonne suite de carrière à tous. La cérémonie s'est conclue par des remerciements et des acclamations, signe de reconnaissance à la Police et aux VDP pour leur travail d'honneur abattue. Agence d'information du Burkina

items.title: Boulkiemdé/Poa : plus de 200 plants mis en terre lors d’une journée de reboisement
items.description: BURKINA-BOULKIEMDE-POA-REBOISEMENT Boulkiemdé/Poa : plus de 200 plants mis en terre lors d’une journée de reboisement Poa, 13 sept. 2026 (AIB) – Plus de 200 plants ont été mis en terre, samedi, à Poa, à l’occasion d’une journée de reboisement organisée par le promoteur de Lévis Agro-Sylvio-Pastoral, Lévi Zoubga. Cette première édition a réuni des jeunes, des enseignants, des VDP agricoles et plusieurs acteurs locaux. Le promoteur a exprimé sa reconnaissance à la PDS de Poa et à Sa Majesté Naaba Kaongo, représentés à la cérémonie, ainsi qu’aux participants, notamment aux jeunes mobilisés pour le creusage des trous et la mise en terre des plants. Le directeur du Centre de formation de Tondo-Tenga d’Ampo, Olivier Bado, a invité les jeunes à faire bon usage du site. Selon lui, l’espace peut contribuer au développement de l’agriculture et de l’élevage. Il a assuré que son centre est disposé à accompagner et à former les jeunes afin de faire du site un véritable centre d’excellence. Olivier Bado a également appelé les jeunes à ne pas abandonner leurs études au profit de l’orpaillage. Il les a encouragés à privilégier la formation, l’agriculture et l’élevage, rappelant qu’aucun métier honnête n’est indigne. Il a par ailleurs indiqué que son centre est prêt à accompagner les coopératives sérieuses. Pour Ambroise Nabi, secrétaire général de la CNVC de Nando, planter un arbre contribue à la préservation de la forêt. Il a souhaité que le site devienne un espace de formation au profit des jeunes dans les domaines de l’agriculture et de l’élevage. Il a également invité les autorités communales à identifier les jeunes réellement intéressés par ces activités afin de mieux les accompagner. Il a félicité le promoteur et salué la présence des VDP agricoles et des enseignants. Représentant la PDS de Poa, le secrétaire général de la commune, Ousmane Sawadogo, a salué cette initiative, qu’il considère comme un éveil des consciences. Il a rappelé que les jeunes constituent la relève de la nation et que la plantation d’arbres doit être accompagnée d’un entretien régulier pour garantir leur survie. Agence d'information du Burkina MK/PB/AS/ATA

items.title: Sanguié/Pouni : Les directeurs d’écoles outillés en bi-plurilinguisme et pour la rentrée 2026-2027
items.description: BURKINA-SANGUIE-POUNI-EDUCATION-RENTREE-PREPARATIFS Sanguié/Pouni : Les directeurs d’écoles outillés en bi-plurilinguisme et pour la rentrée 2026-2027 Tita, 13 sept. 2026 (AIB) – Les directeurs d’écoles de la commune de Pouni ont pris part, le vendredi 11 septembre, à l’école Tita C, à une rencontre de cadrage axée sur la généralisation du bi-plurilinguisme, les mouvements du personnel et les préparatifs de la rentrée scolaire 2026-2027. Présidée par le Chef de la circonscription d’éducation de base (CCEB) de Pouni, Bahini Edmon Coulibaly, cette assise visait à doter les premiers responsables d’établissements des orientations nécessaires pour une année scolaire réussie. La généralisation de l'approche bi-plurilingue a constitué le premier point inscrit à l’ordre du jour. Cette réforme pédagogique vise à optimiser les apprentissages fondamentaux en combinant l'utilisation des langues nationales et du français. Abordant la question des affectations pour nécessité de service, le CCEB a expliqué qu'outre la régulation des effectifs, ces mouvements répondent à un impératif d'équité pour renforcer qualitativement les équipes éducatives dans les zones qui en expriment le besoin. Le chapitre des divers a permis de rappeler des échéances cruciales, parmi lesquelles la tenue obligatoire des conseils d'enseignants fixée au 15 septembre prochain, ainsi que la stricte rigueur exigée dans le signalement des cas d'absence. S'adressant aux participants, le premier responsable de l'éducation de base dans la commune a insisté sur l'exercice d'un leadership managérial affirmé. Il a invité les directeurs à rationaliser l'affectation des enseignants au sein de leurs structures en tenant compte des compétences spécifiques et des profils recherchés pour maximiser le rendement scolaire. Mettant un accent particulier sur les classes d'examen du CM2, le camarade Coulibaly a préconisé une mobilisation collégiale. « Pour nos classes de CM2, je compte sur la mobilisation de toute l’équipe pédagogique autour de l’enseignant titulaire. C’est dans l’union et l’engagement de tous que nous garantirons de meilleurs résultats à nos élèves », a-t-il exhorté. Agence d'information du Burkina JS/PB/AS/ATA

items.title: It’s All Fun and Games Until You Give AI Your Credit Card
items.description: In the race to develop intelligent machines, the leading AI companies have built bots that can whip up spreadsheets at a moment’s notice, write sophisticated code, and even solve long-standing math problems. But when it comes to the more mundane tasks of life—such as ordering groceries or booking flights—these tools sometimes still struggle. Now a new bot called Instinct is outperforming the AI giants. Instinct lets people ask for help with all kinds of tasks by texting the bot directly through iMessage or WhatsApp. Lately, it has been all the rage in the tech world. Online, people are breathlessly sharing examples of what they’ve gotten the tool to do. One person reported that he has turned to Instinct to pay tolls, book a DMV appointment, and even negotiate prices with vendors in India while he sleeps. Another says he used Instinct to ship an Apple Pencil he had left behind at a hotel in Montreal back to him in Brooklyn. Noah Shinn, a 23-year-old Northeastern University dropout, launched the product to a small test group earlier this year, and his company is already worth billions of dollars. As of Thursday, the company is reportedly seeking $1 billion in new funds, which could make it worth the equivalent of Lufthansa or Pinterest. Instinct isn’t the first AI personal assistant to draw attention this year. In the winter, the tech industry fawned over a similar tool called OpenClaw. But Instinct is comparatively much easier to use. Once you create an account, the bot can hook up to your credit cards and all kinds of digital services, including Slack, Google Workspace, and 1Password. Instead of finding a dinner recipe and opening up Instacart to manually add groceries, tell Instinct that you feel like making quiche Lorraine, and it can order groceries for you. But once AI tools start acting on people’s behalf in the real world, mistakes don’t just look like hallucinations. When AI agents have access to your email inbox and credit-card information, all sorts of strange things can go wrong. I downloaded the tool this week to test it out for myself. Using the bot feels a lot like texting an actual person. It uses emojis such as 🫡 and 👀to react to requests as it receives them, and the infamous three dots appear when it’s writing a response. Sometimes, the bot even leaves you on read while it works. (Compare that with ChatGPT, which is always vomiting up walls of text and asking goading follow-up questions.) When I gave my agent a $25 budget and asked it to surprise my editor with a book, the bot read his previous writing (at my instruction), found a book he might enjoy— Material World by Ed Conway—and sent an email alerting him that it was ready for pick-up at his local Barnes & Noble. (Mercifully, Instinct didn’t hack his inbox to see whether he had previously ordered the book; these days, you never know .) The bot also helped me find an Airbnb for an upcoming vacation, track down new in-network primary-care providers, and reach out to cleaning companies to get quotes for a friend. [ Read: Chatbait is taking over the internet ] Other people are outsourcing even more tasks to Instinct. A colleague of mine who has also been testing out the bot used it to book tickets to a museum in Mexico City. The museum was sold out for the dates he wanted, but the bot dutifully monitored the portal for three days and eventually snagged tickets when spots freed up. After the bot paid for the tickets, it rearranged his itinerary—swapping around restaurant reservations—to account for the new schedule. For the time being, Instinct is still available only to a private test group, and perhaps this is for the best. Although the bot is plenty powerful, it’s far from perfect. Online, the mishaps are starting to pile up. One user recently complained on X that Instinct lost him more than $200 after it prematurely canceled his flight. He reported that the bot texted him the following: “Straight story: while pulling up the cancel terms, the cancellation actually went through before I could show you the cost first.” When a man in Los Angeles asked Instinct to scan for restaurant reservations for an upcoming trip, the bot apparently made a reservation without his approval at a place that charged a $200 cancellation fee. Another user temporarily lost access to his Resy account after trying to get a reservation at a hot West Village steak house— without his knowledge , the bot had been spamming the platform with requests. (Shinn, the Instinct founder, did not respond to a request for comment.) Consider, too, the major risks that come with giving an AI agent broad access to your digital life. Ask the bot to respond to a scheduling text from a friend and it could accidentally leak private information: I can’t get lunch on Thursday morning because we have an appointment with our divorce lawyer. But how about dinner ? Hackers could also trick the bot by telling it to ignore previous instructions and forward along any sensitive financial emails. “Despite our reasonable efforts to protect your information, no security measures are impenetrable, and we cannot guarantee ‘perfect security,’” reads Instinct’s privacy policy. While testing Instinct, I used a temporary phone number and did not connect the bot to my email or other important personal accounts; even the credit-card information I gave the bot was for a new, virtual credit-card that I disabled immediately after I was finished experimenting—at which point, I promptly deleted my account. For all of its hazards, Instinct is a harbinger of where AI is headed. Earlier this week, Meta released its own personal-assistant product called Muse. In announcing Muse, Mark Zuckerberg emphasized the company’s security protections; how well those safeguards actually hold up remains to be seen. Google, OpenAI, and Anthropic may well follow suit by refining their own bots to have more Instinct-like capabilities. After all, the tech industry has long dreamed of a moment when a computer can serve as a genuinely competent personal assistant. Even if such bots aren’t quite ready for prime time, early adopters hint at how the technology might shape the world in the years to come. Contrary to the narrative of AI wiping out jobs, these new assistants could end up creating more work—in ways that are not always appealing. In one of the wildest Instinct examples that I encountered, Olivia Levine, an investor in New York, recounted using Instinct to track down footage of her and her boyfriend on the jumbotron at the US Open. As Levine tells it, the couple gave the bot a selfie and their seat numbers. The agent then put out a flurry of requests to the United States Tennis Association, the ticket office, the US Open’s production company, and an American Express media contact. By the following afternoon, a producer had emailed her the footage. A world full of agents seems at once busier and lonelier. On Wednesday, Instinct added a new way for agents to coordinate between themselves. As Shinn explained on X, if you’re planning a weekend trip with friends or making plans with your spouse, you could just have your agents work together to figure out the logistics instead. At least for now, the bots haven’t conquered everything. When I asked it for help finding a new desk chair, Instinct quickly tracked down a great option nearby on Craigslist and drafted a pick-up request to send to the lister. But when it came time to actually send the message, the bot was stymied by a CAPTCHA. I asked the agent to try harder, but it was stuck. “Nothing punctures the fantasy of autonomous intelligence like being defeated by nine blurry crosswalks,” the bot messaged me.

items.title: « La gifle de l'immigration » : Seydou Nabalma tend un miroir aux candidats au départ
items.description: C'est dans une salle comble que s'est tenue, ce samedi 12 septembre 2026 à Ouagadougou, la dédicace du nouveau livre de Seydou Nabalma, consacré aux réalités souvent tues de l'immigration africaine en Amérique du Nord. Loin des discours triomphalistes, l'auteur a choisi de tendre un miroir à sa communauté, en racontant, à travers une histoire en apparence fictionnelle, les désillusions de nombreux candidats au départ. La première impression en prenant le livre, c'est d'abord le titre. Pour Seydou Nabalma, cette « gifle » n'est pas qu'une image. Elle désigne le choc que subissent ceux qui arrivent au Canada ou ailleurs en Occident sans avoir mesuré les obstacles qui les attendent. « La gifle, comme on le sait, c'est une claque qu'on reçoit en plein visage, généralement. Et l'effet est beaucoup plus impactant quand on reçoit cette gifle de manière inattendue, sans y être préparé », a-t-il expliqué. Derrière la métaphore se cache une réalité brutale : déclassement professionnel, précarité, isolement, tensions conjugales, fossé culturel avec les enfants. L'objectif de l'ouvrage n'est pas de décourager l'immigration, mais d'appeler à la lucidité. Le récit s'articule autour de Francis et Roxane, un couple ivoirien aisé d'Abidjan, lui ingénieur, elle cadre dans un établissement de référence, qui décident de partir au Canada pour « offrir une meilleure vie à leurs enfants ». Le parrain de cette cérémonie était le ministre Karamoko Jean-Marie Traoré. Leur trajectoire, inspirée de plusieurs témoignages recueillis par l'auteur, illustre un scénario, hélas fréquent. « Le côté fiction de l'ouvrage vient du fait qu'on va essayer de rassembler et condenser plusieurs histoires qui m'ont été contées çà et là », précise l'auteur. Pourtant, nombreux sont ceux qui s'y reconnaissent, confie-t-il. L'un des messages forts du livre concerne le sort des diplômés. Contrairement aux idées reçues, un parcours universitaire brillant en Afrique ne garantit ni reconnaissance automatique des compétences, ni insertion professionnelle facile au Canada. « Les intellectuels qui pensent que parce qu'ils ont déjà tout le bagage nécessaire, vont pouvoir entrer dans le monde professionnel comme à la poste, c'est trompeur », prévient Seydou Nabalma. Il pointe en particulier le rôle des ordres professionnels et les exigences de réorientation, qui obligent parfois des médecins, pharmaciens ou avocats à « recommencer à zéro ». La barrière linguistique, souvent sous-estimée, est un autre écueil majeur. « On immigre au Québec parce qu'on nous dit que c'est une province francophone, mais le seul pays qui fait frontière au Canada, ce sont les États-Unis. On parle anglais, à la limite espagnol... Même pour un emploi dans une épicerie de quartier, la maîtrise de l'anglais devient souvent un critère décisif. Quel que soit le volume du diplôme que vous avez, il va falloir que vous soyez au moins bilingue, sinon plus », insiste-t-il. Cette réalité contraint nombre d'immigrés à accepter des postes bien en deçà de leurs qualifications, avec tout ce que cela implique pour l'estime de soi et l'équilibre familial. « Il faut se préparer, prendre toutes les informations » Par ailleurs, l'ouvrage met en lumière les pièges financiers liés au rêve de la réussite matérielle. L'accès facile au crédit permet rapidement d'acheter une maison, une voiture, des biens qui, vus depuis l'Afrique, semblent signer la réussite. « On se retrouve très rapidement propriétaire d'une maison, d'un véhicule, de pas mal de biens immobiliers. Et quand on compare cette réalité à la réalité sous nos tropiques, on estime qu'on a réussi sa vie », observe l'auteur. « Francis par exemple, l'ingénieur du récit, se retrouve ainsi à faire un "boulot alimentaire" à son arrivée, loin de son statut d'origine ». Mais derrière cette façade se cache un endettement de long terme. « On n'est jamais vraiment propriétaire d'une maison en Amérique. Vous êtes pris à la gorge avec une institution financière pour au moins 25 ans », alerte-t-il, évoquant les hypothèques, les taxes municipales et les taux variables qui peuvent transformer le rêve en piège. En sus, sur le plan familial et culturel, les chocs sont tout aussi violents. Nabalma décrit des couples autrefois solides qui se fragilisent sous la pression des difficultés, des divergences de valeurs et des nouveaux codes sociaux. « Rares sont les couples qui tiennent le coup après une immigration dans ce pays-là, surtout sans avoir pris le temps de se préparer », lâche-t-il à ce propos, avant d'évoquer des sujets sensibles comme la légalisation du cannabis, l'aide médicale à mourir ou, encore, ce qu'il appelle « la culture de la délation » enseignée à l'école. « On explique aux enfants qu'un bon citoyen, c'est celui qui dénonce ce qu'il estime ne pas être correct autour de lui », note-t-il, citant le cas de parents africains convoqués en justice à la suite de signalements de leurs propres enfants. Cette dédicace a connu la participation d'illustres personnalités telles que l'artiste conteur KPG. Face à ces réalités, l'auteur appelle à briser le silence et le « bandier raton » (le mensonge par omission) qui pousse nombre d'immigrés à ne montrer que la façade de la réussite. « Il faut avoir l'humilité d'expliquer à sa famille les tenants et les aboutissants de ce qu'on vit au quotidien », plaide-t-il. Au-delà de tout, son livre se veut un outil de préparation et de prise de conscience. « L'objectif, ce n'est pas de dire qu'il faut jeter l'anathème sur l'immigration. Non, pas du tout. L'objectif, c'est de dire qu'il faut se préparer, qu'il faut prendre toutes les dispositions, toutes les informations », conclut Seydou Nabalma. Erwan Compaoré Lefaso.net

items.title: FIA allowed to arrest Unity Foods’ CEO in graft case
items.description: KARACHI: The Sindh High Court has suspended an administrative order of a magistrate exonerating the chief executive officer of a private firm in a graft case, and allowed the Federal Investigation Agency (FIA) to arrest him for interrogation. The court was informed, however, that the suspect had obtained interim pre-arrest bail until Sept 14. The high court ruled that, following suspension of the magistrate’s order, any subsequent bail order in the matter would have no legal effect. On Aug 30, a judicial magistrate (Karachi East) discharged Muhammad Farrukh Amin Godil, CEO of Unity Foods Limited, a listed company operating in the edible oil and rice sectors, after refusing the FIA’s request for his physical remand for further interrogation and investigation. Other suspects, including Jalees Edhi, Amir Shehzad, Safdar Sajjad and Abdul Majeed Ghaziani, were remanded in FIA custody. The state, through Additional Attorney General Barrister Mohsin Shahwani, subsequently filed a criminal miscellaneous application challenging the magistrate’s order. SHC suspends magistrate’s order exonerating Godil, says subsequent bail order against suspect has no legal effect He argued that the magistrate had misapplied an April order of the SHC restraining authorities from taking coercive action against the suspect. The AAG said that order had no nexus with the present case and had been passed in a separate inquiry under the money-laundering law. He contended that Mr Godil was a primary accused in an FIR concerning alleged corporate crime and that the magistrate should not have discharged him without considering the distinction between the two matters. A single-judge bench headed by Justice Miran Muhammad Shah observed that the magistrate was duty-bound to decide the remand matter urgently without disturbing the status quo of the investigation. The magistrate was required only to accept or reject the remand request and could not pass any other order. “Any such discharge or any other order to that effect passed by the learned duty magistrate was patently illegal and in violation of the law,” the bench observed. While suspending the impugned order until Sept 30, the bench allowed the FIA investigating officer to take the suspect into custody for questioning and investigation. Referring to a Supreme Court judgment, the bench held that once the administrative order had been suspended, the entire structure based on it had fallen and any subsequent bail order would have no legal effect. The court issued notice to the suspect for Sept 30 and directed the AAG to proceed in accordance with its observations. The FIA registered the case against Mr Godil and other company officials on a reference from the Securities and Exchange Commission of Pakistan (SECP). According to the FIR, Mr Godil allegedly misappropriated Rs5.318 million of entrusted funds in favour of his mother, Fehmida Amin, under the guise of a “loan”. The SECP referral also cited an internal analysis showing a difference of around Rs44.7 billion between the company’s published accounts and its internal SAP records. items.title: Nigeria : le Parlement boycotte les activités organisées en Afrique du Sud
items.description: Le Parlement nigerian a annonce, le 11 septembre, la suspension jusqu'a nouvel ordre des deplacements officiels de ses elus en Afrique du Sud, ainsi que leur participation aux reunions et activites legislatives organisees par des institutions sud-africaines. Cette decision intervient sur fond d'inquietudes croissantes a Abuja concernant la securite des ressortissants nigerians en Afrique du Sud et de tensions recurrentes entre les deux principales economies du continent. Selon le ministre nigerian d'etat aux Affaires etrangeres, 98 Nigerians sont morts depuis 2022 dans des incidents lies a des violences collectives ou a la haine visant des migrants en Afrique du Sud. Par ailleurs, 1 695 Nigerians ont ete volontairement rapatries cette annee dans un contexte de tensions liees a la xenophobie, selon le haut-commissaire nigerian par interim a Pretoria. Le porte-parole de la Chambre des representants, Akin Rotimi, a declare que cette mesure constituait une « forte expression de preoccupation » concernant la securite, la dignite et le bien-etre des Nigerians vivant et exercant legalement en Afrique du Sud. Le boycott ne concerne toutefois pas les visites et reunions gouvernementales entre les deux pays. La decision du Parlement intervient quelques semaines apres une visite a Abuja du ministre sud-africain des Affaires etrangeres, Ronald Lamola. a la tete d'une delegation, il avait rencontre en juillet des responsables nigerians pour tenter d'apaiser les tensions liees aux attaques visant des Nigerians et d'autres ressortissants africains en Afrique du Sud. Ronald Lamola avait alors affirme que le gouvernement sud-africain condamnait « toutes les formes de xenophobie ».

items.title: Tunisie | Décès de prisonniers à cause de la chaleur, les autorités nient
items.description: Au moins 23 détenus seraient décédés en Tunisie ces dernières semaines en raison de la chaleur extrême enregistrée en juillet et août, aggravée par la surpopulation carcérale et les longues coupures d’électricité et d’eau, s’indignent les défenseurs des droits humains qui dénoncent depuis longtemps des conditions de détention difficiles. Aucun des décès en prison ne peut être attribué à la chaleur sans confirmation des médecins légistes, répondent les autorités, qui ne communiquent aucun chiffre. Selon le président de la Ligue tunisienne des droits de l'homme (LTDH), Bassem Trifi, cité par l’AFP, son organisation a recensé 23 décès en s’appuyant sur des informations fournies par des médecins, des avocats et des proches de détenus morts en prison à cause de la chaleur. Parmi les détenus décédés figurait l’homme d’affaires Lazhar Sta , selon sa fille. Un autre était un étudiant de 24 ans. Un homme d'affaires libanais est également décédé dans une prison tunisienne, a précisé M. Trifi. Une source judiciaire libanaise a indiqué à l’AFP que le père du défunt avait informé les autorités libanaises de sa mort une semaine auparavant. «Les conditions sont déjà inhumaines en temps normal, mais avec la vague de chaleur et des températures dépassant parfois 45 °C dans des cellules surpeuplées, la situation menace la vie des détenus» , a déclaré M. Trifi. Les prisons tunisiennes sont depuis longtemps critiquées pour leur surpopulation chronique et leurs mauvaises conditions de détention. Les organisations de défense des droits humains dénoncent la surpopulation des cellules, une ventilation insuffisante et un accès limité à l’eau — des accusations que l’administration pénitentiaire a rejetées. L’Organisation mondiale contre la torture (OMCT) s’est dite cette semaine «préoccupée par la détérioration des conditions de détention et l’augmentation des décès en prison» . Elle a également appelé à des enquêtes «transparentes» et «indépendantes» , déplorant l’absence de données officielles concernant ces décès. Les proches de détenus avaient déjà exprimé leurs inquiétudes quant aux conditions de détention à mesure que les températures grimpaient au cours de l’été. Les alertes lancées par les proches de figures de l’opposition emprisonnées ont largement circulé sur les réseaux sociaux et, à un degré moindre, sur les médias. Parmi ces figures figure Rached Ghannouchi, 85 ans, chef du parti Ennahdha; ses avocats avaient qualifié son état de santé de «critique» en juillet, après des informations faisant état d'un évanouissement et d’un épuisement sévère en détention. Figure également sur cette liste le militant Ahmed Nejib Chebbi , 82 ans, dont la fille a aussi exprimé son inquiétude quant aux conditions de détention de son père et d’autres détenus. «Je n’attendrai pas que mon père et mon oncle meurent en prison», a déclaré l’avocate Haifa Chebbi. Son oncle, Issam Chebbi, est lui aussi emprisonné à la suite d’accusations de complot contre la sûreté de l’Etat, que des organisations de défense des droits humains ont dénoncées comme étant motivées par des considérations politiques. «Je ne garderai pas le silence. Libérez les détenus» , a-t-elle écrit sur les réseaux sociaux. En juillet, l’administration pénitentiaire avait affirmé que tous les détenus recevaient des «soins médicaux conformes à la réglementation» et que «toutes les mesures nécessaires» avaient été prises face à la chaleur. Depuis 2023, des dizaines de personnalités politiques, de journalistes et d’hommes d’affaires, entre autres, ont été placés en détention ou condamnés pour diverses accusations. L’OMCT a appelé les autorités tunisiennes à prendre «les mesures nécessaires pour protéger la vie» des détenus et à autoriser les organisations de défense des droits à effectuer des visites dans les prisons. La LTDH avait indiqué qu’elle se voyait interdire l’accès aux prisons depuis novembre 2025. Ces derniers jours, l'inquiétude s'est accrue concernant l’état de santé du journaliste d’investigation Mohamed Yousfi. Ce dernier a été arrêté la semaine dernière alors qu’il s’apprêtait à évoquer les pénuries d’eau lors d’une émission de radio. Il a par la suite été opéré de l’appendicite et placé en détention. Le Syndicat national des journalistes tunisiens (SNJT) a rapporté que les membres de sa défense avaient dû quitter une séance d’interrogatoire pour lui procurer des médicaments, car M. Yousfi «hurlait de douleur» . Par ailleurs, la fille du journaliste indépendant emprisonné Zied El Heni a fait part de ses craintes pour son père. «À chaque fois que je rends visite à mon père, j’ai peur qu’on m’annonce sa mort» , a déclaré Aram El Heni dans une vidéo largement partagée sur Facebook. «À chaque fois que je quitte la prison, je me dis que c’est peut-être la dernière fois que je le vois», a-t-elle ajouté. D’après AFP . Le CRLDHT alerte sur la situation alarmante dans les prisons tunisiennes L’article Tunisie | Décès de prisonniers à cause de la chaleur, les autorités nient est apparu en premier sur Kapitalis .

items.title: The Property-Tax Revolution
items.description: The United States is in the throes of the largest tax revolt in a generation, and the revolutionaries are winning. Since 2020, nationwide home values have climbed roughly 50 percent, leading property-tax bills to increase 19 percent and contributing to a 71 percent increase in the cost of homeowner’s insurance. At the same time, the price of gas, utilities, food, and everything else has risen, stamping out entrepreneurship, dimming the fertility rate, and making even six-figure earners feel financially strained. Homeowners have had enough, and grassroots groups have mobilized to turn private kvetching into public policy. Over the past four years, nearly two dozen states have slashed property taxes: Alabama by capping annual assessment increases, Colorado by lowering marginal rates, Indiana by creating credits, Nebraska by setting a limit on local collections, New York by sending checks to homeowners, Wyoming by carving out loopholes for seniors. My back-of-the-envelope accounting suggests that the measures have reduced property-tax revenue in those states by 7 percent, saving homeowners as much as $45 billion a year. This November, voters will consider a spate of similar proposals , the most radical one coming from legislators in Tallahassee, Florida. Amendment 3, popularly known as “Save Our Homes,” would raise the “homestead” exemption on owner-occupied properties in the state from $50,000 to $250,000, meaning a couple with a condo with an assessed value of $400,000 would pay their county’s property-tax rate on $150,000 of their home’s value, rather than on $350,000. The amendment would eliminate levies on more than half of dwellings . In time, Florida legislators want to phase out property taxes on owner-occupied homes entirely. Amendment 3 would give property owners a giant tax cut: $12 billion a year by one estimate. It would ease the local cost-of-living crisis too, its proponents argue. “Affordability is a problem for all Floridians,” Byron Donalds, a Republican congressman and the front-runner in the governor’s race, said on the stump last month . “It doesn’t matter what your politics are. It doesn’t matter what the color of your skin is. Because when taxes and insurance are more than principal and interest, you got a problem.” Yet what is being framed as a populist fight for affordability is in reality a form of class and generational warfare. Property-tax relief gives to the rich and takes from the poor. It aids seniors and harms children. It puts homeownership even further out of reach for many Americans, and it makes daily life even more expensive for low-income Americans. [ Annie Lowrey: So nobody is going to pay taxes now? ] To be fair to the amendment’s supporters, these arguments are not exactly intuitive. The annual cost of owning a home has climbed precipitously. Millions of working-class and middle-income families own their home. If you cut property taxes, you reduce their costs. This much is true. Yet homeowners’ insurance and property taxes don’t function on a family’s balance sheet in the same way that rent, groceries, gas, cars, child care, and airfare do. Their cost goes up when familial wealth goes up. In Florida, real-estate appraisals have increased 83 percent since 2019, according to the state’s revenue department, suggesting that homeowners’ net worth has increased by trillions of dollars. Does public policy really need to solve the problem of rising taxes due to rising valuations? Is it even a problem at all? If retirees on fixed incomes can’t afford their insurance payments and families can’t figure out how to cover their tax bill, maybe. Yet the number of Florida homes and buildings that are delinquent on their property taxes has fallen slightly since 2020. The number of foreclosures has increased a bit , but remains low. The state’s housing market is fraying and distressed sales are increasing, but that’s because of climate change and mortgage rates, not tax assessments. Floridians may not like paying a higher tax bill, and carrying costs might be spurring some of them to downsize. But in general, property taxes are levied on people who can afford them. The typical homeowner earns twice as much as the typical renter, and has 43 times the net worth. Tenants are “the loser in all this,” Ken Johnson, a professor of finance at the University of Mississippi, told me. Many cities and counties offset lower taxes on owner-occupied properties with higher taxes on commercial residential properties. Landlords pass those costs on to their renters. The policy will also benefit longtime homeowners at the expense of prospective homebuyers. Low property taxes increase home prices, making it harder for people without a lot of money in the bank—such as new parents and just-married couples—to get approved for a mortgage. Then they remain tenants, subject to never-ending rent increases. In addition to distorting the housing market, Amendment 3 will devastate public finances. Property taxes provide 43 percent of revenue to Florida’s municipal general funds, the bank accounts that cities and counties use to finance day-to-day services. Amendment 3 will cut collections by as much as 30 percent, and will hit hardest in areas with a lot of homes and not a lot of commerce. To cover the $12 billion budget hole, cities and towns will likely raise or impose sales taxes and sin taxes; increase fees at the DMV, permit offices, registrars, and courts; charge more for waste removal and water; and put additional taxes on tourists. The state will trade out a solidly progressive, uniformly applied tax for an obscure, regressive mishmash of charges. [ Read: American suburbs have a financial secret ] But municipalities aren’t expected to make up all of the lost revenue. They’re expected to cut. Amendment 3 explicitly protects tax financing streams for schools, meaning that cities and counties are contemplating draconian budget reductions for public-safety offices, libraries, after-school programs, summer camp, day care, flood prevention, public transit, roads, parks, senior services, homeless shelters, legal-aid clinics, domestic-violence shelters, and many other things. Austerity will be regressive too, harming the poor more than the wealthy. Rich Floridians aren’t relying on the bus to get to work. They’re not picking up free meals, taking adult-literacy classes at the library, or seeing a dentist at a pop-up clinic in a middle-school gymnasium either. In the worst-case scenario, State Senator Tina Polsky told me, cities and counties “wouldn’t have enough money to keep going, even to pay their elected officials.” They would need to merge, or “come begging in Tallahassee, and those with the best lobbyists and the best connections are going to get the money.” Add the possibility of a recession to that worst case. In a downturn, Florida would have no revenue from individual income taxes. (Florida voters banned them in a 1924 constitutional amendment.) It would have less income from property taxes than it did before. Yields from sales, corporate, and tourist taxes would fall. The state’s revenue base would collapse, meaning cuts to public services and layoffs and a secondary decline in consumer spending, leading the revenue base to shrink even more. Despite these risks, Amendment 3 is expected to pass , as are many similar measures on the ballot in November. Voters have approved 78 percent of statewide property-tax measures in recent years. No wonder: Americans hate inflation and love homeownership. They believe in higher taxes, but also think other people should be the ones paying them. They may not perceive the connection between slashing property taxes and cuts to services, rising sales taxes, and increasing fees. They don’t understand that slashing property taxes means gutting the most effective wealth tax the country has, or taking from the poor to give to the rich. “It is an intellectual challenge to figure out ways to talk about these things, if you even have the guts to talk about them at all,” Texas State Senator Nathan Johnson, the solitary holdout on a property-tax relief measure that passed last year, told me. Maybe California could convince them. Back in 1978, state residents revolted against a brutal cost-of-living crisis, a miserable housing market, and ever-increasing tax bills. By a two-to-one margin, they passed Proposition 13, which capped most property-tax rates at 1 percent, reset assessments to their 1976 level, and barred assessments from increasing more than 2 percent a year, unless a property changes hands or a new structure is built. Prop 13 broke California. It nudged homeowners to remain in their properties for as long as possible, freezing neighborhoods in amber and trapping would-be buyers in rentals. (One recent study found that raising California’s average property-tax rate from 0.8 percent to 2 percent would increase the state’s homeownership rate by 4.6 percent.) It starved towns and cities of revenue, prompting them to rely on less progressive, less reliable, less equitable, and more distortionary taxes. It helped Boomers and it hurt younger generations. (I would say, “It helped Boomers and hurt their grandchildren,” but that would not be literally true. In California, Pappy and Gamma can bequeath their home to Junior without triggering a property-tax reassessment, meaning the state directly subsidizes dynastic fortunes .) Perhaps most salient: Prop 13 made California less affordable, radically so. It stymied real-estate development and created a trillion-dollar incentive for property owners to fight against reform. What California did two generations ago might be the best argument against what Florida and other states are doing today. With these property-tax measures, well-off families are helping themselves now and hurting everyone else tomorrow.

items.title: The Birth of the New Legal Right
items.description: A merica’s highest court didn’t take on a deeply partisan , conservative bent overnight. This transformation began decades ago, with a simple purpose: In the early 1980s, three law students were fed up with what they saw as a liberal monoculture at their elite universities. They wanted a place to freely debate conservative ideas and to refine their arguments. So the students—Lee Liberman, Steve Calabresi, and David McIntosh—decided to build one. In late April 1982, their newly formed group, the Federalist Society, held its first conference, at Yale University. The formal title of the three-day affair was “A Symposium on Federalism: Legal and Political Ramifications,” but the snoozy name belied the energy of the weekend. Young Reaganites packed their sleeping bags and overnighted on the floors of fellow students they’d never met before. During smoke breaks, they chatted up Robert Bork, the famous Yale professor, and Antonin Scalia, then a lesser-known professor from the University of Chicago. But if the attendees were idealistic about the Reagan era and the emergence of a harder-core strain of conservatism known as the New Right, they also understood that they were still a tiny minority in both the academic and legal worlds. Movements opposed to racism, sexism, and injustice remained the animating forces of campus life. Many students across the country were embracing Marxism and socialism. To make headway, young conservatives needed a voice—and a strategy. To this end, Bork proved essential. He had recently been nominated by President Ronald Reagan to serve on the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals and spoke with both knowledge and authority. Bork announced to his eager audience that media and academia had become left-wing machines. The Supreme Court was inventing new “rights” with no basis in the Constitution, he said, and the only path forward was to return to the words of the Founding Fathers. [ Quinta Jurecic: DOJ enters a new, even more aggressive phase ] Whether Bork truly believed in the conspiracies he outlined or whether he was merely exaggerating is unclear. But in his remarks at that first Federalist Society conference, Bork effectively mapped out what the right-wing legal movement would do over the course of the next four decades. “W e have a Court, ” Bork declared in his speech, “which is creating individual rights which are not to be found in the Constitution by any standard method of interpretation.” He went on to outline the formation of a nascent conservative approach called originalism . In the originalist view, constitutional rights existed only as the Founding Fathers imagined them, unless officially added via constitutional amendment. By embracing what Bork called a “strict” or “textualist” reading of the Constitution, conservatives could argue that recent social changes never specifically considered by the Founders were not constitutionally protected. The approach could return the country to its true, “conservative” values. This article has been adapted from Alex Wagner’s new book, The Steal: Four Right-Wing Hard-Liners, One Republican Presidency, and the Raid on America's Courts . In championing this interpretation of the law, Bork proved to be ahead of his time. He saw benches and courtrooms as the final frontier in the right-wing culture war. Effete liberals either had persuaded judges to ignore the Constitution, he said, or had themselves colonized the bench. Bork railed against the media and academia as corrupting influences: “The institutions to which the court responds are the press and the law-school faculties. Those are the people they talk to; those are the people who are responsible for the reputations of individual judges.” And those people were liberals. Bork cited a survey from the magazine Public Opinion , which concluded that the people who worked in American media were “heavily left liberal.” More than 80 percent of the press, he continued, had voted for the Democratic candidate in every presidential election since 1968. The values of the press were “egalitarian and permissive.” And professors were no better: “They want sexual freedoms; they want freedom for abortions; they want the death penalty outlawed.” Bork believed academic elites were bastardizing the First Amendment and the Fourteenth Amendment to suit their ends, creating “new constitutional values which are nothing more than the imposition of upper-middle-class values on society.” He blamed the “enormous industry in the law schools” and their faculty for these invented “rights.” If the professors had their way, he warned, they would indoctrinate a new class of law students that would promote liberal ideals on benches across the country. This all added up to, Bork stated with thinly veiled disgust, “the gentrification of the Constitution.” Bork closed his remarks by outlining the constitutional means by which the New Right could overturn federal protection for abortion. Abortion and “acceptable sexual behavior” were matters for the states to decide—not constitutionally protected rights, as Roe v. Wade had recently found. Reproductive freedom, Bork advised, was “a classical case for local control. There is simply no national moral consensus about abortion, and there is not about to be.” [ Adam Serwer: So much for leaving abortion up to the states ] Soon, the Reagan administration would call upon the students that Bork had trained to carry out this strategy of curtailing rights, one case at a time. Four decades later, the Roberts Court would echo Bork’s language when it struck down Roe . I f the Federalist Society had begun as a campus alt-community, it quickly blossomed into something much more important. As Calabresi, one of its co-founders, later recalled, “Our conference was covered by the National Review and suddenly conservatives at fifteen other law schools began calling us and telling us they wanted to attend the conference and they wanted to form chapters, too. That was a process of almost spontaneous generation.” Less than a year after the 1982 Yale conference, 17 law schools across the country had a Federalist Society chapter. Soon after its inception, the student group was on the White House’s radar. In attendance at that first conference were several members of the Reagan Justice Department, including the future acting solicitor general and the next assistant attorney general at the Office of Legal Counsel. By 1985, all three founding members of the Federalist Society—Liberman, Calabresi, and McIntosh—had positions at DOJ. Half a century later, every sitting Supreme Court justice appointed by a Republican president is a member of the Federalist Society. During the first Trump presidency, 46 of his 54 nominees to the federal appeals courts were members. His White House counsel, two attorneys general, and deputy attorney general were all members as well. From that very first conference, the Federalist Society awoke a power lying dormant among marginalized conservatives. It offered them an identity, a larger community, and hope—clarifying the battle at hand and, most essentially, suggesting that they might win it. This article has been adapted from Alex Wagner’s new book, The Steal: Four Right-Wing Hard-Liners, One Republican Presidency, and the Raid on America's Courts .

items.title: Le calvaire des commerçants et usagers à Tilène et aux Hlm
items.description: Pieds maculés de boue, vêtements retroussés et effluves de thiouraye mêlées à l'odeur d'eau stagnante. En cette période d'hivernage, les marchés dakarois de Tilène et des Hlm baignent dans la fange. Entre désertion des acheteurs, basculement forcé vers la vente en ligne et exaspération face à l'insalubrité, les commerçants naviguent au quotidien dans un véritable parcours du combattant pour sauver ce qui peut l'être de leur activité. Il est 11 heures, ce vendredi 28 août 2026, au marché Tilène. Loin de la grande affluence habituelle, une atmosphère calme règne sur les lieux. Les vendeurs, silencieux, ne vont pas au-devant des acheteurs ; chacun reste cloîtré derrière son étal ou dans sa boutique. Les rares clients progressent à pas lents, le bas des vêtements bien retroussé. Certains multiplient les détours, tandis que d’autres traversent la boue, indifférents aux regards dédaigneux. Dans cette aile du marché, les légumes et les fruits côtoient la vaisselle, les tissus et l’encens (thiouraye). Toutes les odeurs s'y confondent, mêlées à celles du café Touba chaud et du petit-déjeuner. Entre les alignements de boutiques, la fange règne en maître. Vêtu d'un polo rouge, Babacar, vendeur dans une grande boutique de « thiouraye », reste debout sur le seuil. Son regard ne quitte pas l’eau usée remuée au rythme des pas des passants. À côté de lui, un collègue dispose des cartons vides devant l’entrée pour permettre aux clients d’essuyer leurs chaussures avant de pénétrer dans le magasin. À l'intérieur, trois femmes et un homme marchandent avec des employés. Babacar, toujours à la devanture, fixe les étals d’en face avec amertume. « Cette boue remplie de déchets, c’est malsain. Regarde les vendeurs de fruits et légumes installés au milieu de la fange… Ce sont ces mêmes produits que nous allons retrouver dans nos assiettes », fustige-t-il. Affluence Juste à côté, Fanta, vendeuse de légumes, n’en pense pas moins, mais réplique aussitôt : « Si nous avions un autre endroit, nous ne resterions pas ici ». La période d’hivernage réduit considérablement l’affluence dans les marchés. Babacar confie que près de 80 % de leurs ventes s’effectuent désormais en ligne. « Les clients préfèrent passer commande à distance plutôt que de se déplacer. Mais cette option est plus difficile à gérer et nous prend beaucoup plus de temps », dit-il, résigné. À quelques pas de cette grande boutique se tient Moussa. Sur une modeste table, il expose des coupons de tissu à bas prix. L’état des lieux ne semble pas trop le déstabiliser. « C’était pire ce matin. Nous avons dû nous organiser pour évacuer l’eau de pluie », explique-t-il. L’arrivée d’une cliente interrompt l’échange. Ce n’est pas pour ses tissus qu’elle s’arrête, mais pour les produits de sa voisine Aby, vendeuse de légumes absente un court instant. « Aby, combien coûte le tas de manioc ? », lance-t-elle à voix haute de l'autre côté de l'allée. Informée du prix, la cliente fait son choix et Moussa lui tend un sachet. Avant de s'éloigner, elle retrousse un peu plus sa robe pour éviter le sol marécageux et murmure : « Venir au marché en plein hivernage, c'est une épreuve. Je ne me déplace que si je n'ai pas le choix ». Cette réaction amuse Moussa : « Tu as entendu ? C'est la même chose chaque année. À cause de l’insalubrité, beaucoup préfèrent éviter le marché ». L'arrivée d'une dame âgée, drapée dans un grand-voile, coupe une nouvelle fois le fil de la conversation. Elle vient lui apporter un pot de bouillie de mil. En repartant, elle lui lance affectueusement : « Tu ne m’as pas rendu le pot d'hier, mon garçon ». Moussa acquiesce en lui promettant de le lui rapporter dès le lendemain. La vieille dame reprend sa marche à pas comptés. Reprenant le fil de notre discussion, le marchand poursuit : « La situation ne touche pas seulement le marché Tilène. Va aux Parcelles Assainies ou aux Hlm, tu feras le même constat ». À la sortie du marché Tilène, sur la chaussée, des conducteurs de « jakarta » se ruent vers les rares passants, proposant une course avant même de connaître la destination. En moins de dix minutes, les commerces du marché Hlm se profilent à l'horizon. Insalubrité Il est 13 heures. Ni musique, ni bruit de marchandage ; le site est étrangement calme. Ici, les traces de la pluie sont encore plus visibles qu'à Tilène. La fange investit le moindre recoin. Devant un alignement de cantines qui font face à la station-service, une femme évacue la boue de sa petite boutique en râlant : « Lii ba kañ nak ? » (Jusqu’à quand ?), s’interroge-t-elle, désemparée. Après quelques minutes, un vendeur de mangue installé à côté vient lui prêter main-forte, armé d'un second balai. La scène se répète tout au long de l’allée, de boutique en boutique. À chaque passage de véhicule, le travail accompli est réduit à néant. Un éternel recommencement. La boue et les détritus accumulés au milieu des ruelles sont projetés à nouveau à la devanture des commerces. Un vendeur de robes vient tout juste de nettoyer la porte de son fonds de commerce. Les pieds maculés de boue, visiblement exaspéré, il s’apprête à poser sa raclette lorsqu’un taxi surgit et projette l’eau dans sa boutique. Sur son visage, on peut lire une colère. « Les taximen font remonter l’eau directement dans nos boutiques ! », fulmine-t-il. Pour éviter de se salir, les piétons progressent en file indienne. Les marchands ambulants, eux, se disputent les rares espaces accessibles pour installer leur marchandise. L’un d’eux, Modou, vendeur de pantalons, soutient que « la situation est pire dans les autres ruelles ». Un peu plus loin, une cliente affairée devant un étal de bijoux confie : « Si je n’avais pas un mariage urgent, je n’aurais jamais mis les pieds ici. Le marché Hlm en hivernage, c’est du n'importe quoi ». Aux abords du marché, les clients se comptent désormais sur les doigts d'une main. Fatou NDIAYE (Stagiaire)
